title: Persecution and the Destruction of Skala’s Jews
summary: The wartime accounts document how occupation, forced labor, deportations, and mass murder devastated Skala and its Jewish residents.

## Between Soviet rule and German occupation

The destruction of Skala’s Jews unfolded through a succession of regimes, orders, roundups and killings—not in one event. The memorial book dates the German occupation broadly from late June 1941 to late March 1944. But its chapter, “The Destruction of Skala,” gives a more precise local sequence: it says [Hungarian troops entered Skala on July 8, 1941](/communities/skala/records/event_candidate_cd0894f683aa19878d0eb99d), before German authorities took over the region. These accounts need not be collapsed into one date: the record describes the occupation period generally, while the chapter distinguishes the Hungarian arrival from the later German regime.

The book recalls that Skala had been annexed to the Soviet Union and Soviet Ukraine in September 1939, after a period as part of eastern Poland. The occupation years began with another rupture: the German invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941. The memorial-book chapter describes the Soviet administration’s departure, fear of reprisals, and looting as authority broke down. It also remembers the town’s Jewish residents as a community forced to navigate successive governments while trying to preserve family and communal life.

The book’s account places local experience within a broader history of German persecution, but the distinction matters. The Nazi authorities and their partners imposed the system; local officials, police, and intermediaries enforced measures in Skala and the surrounding district. The town’s [Jewish community](/communities/skala/records/mention_4d24297290f1a4fed1e56c40) was not simply a passive subject of these policies: people warned one another, sought food and release for prisoners, and tried to survive.

## Forced labor and the Judenrat’s impossible choices

The memorial book describes the [Judenrat](/communities/skala/records/mention_3dedc3e340b531fb3961c7d9) as an institution ordered to carry out German demands. In late 1941, Jewish men and women were registered for forced labor, including at Borki-Wielkie. In February 1942, the authorities demanded another quota for [Borki camp](/communities/skala/records/mention_fb3c4ff8cd09361ed123e72c). The book records that the council tried to avert the order, but the demand was enforced with help from the Jewish [Ordnungsdienst](/communities/skala/records/mention_17325cef6571b4d0e72409e9) and Ukrainian police.

The chapter gives this coercion a family face. Uziel Stock carried food parcels to the camp and brought home the body of his son Moshe Stock, who had died there in a work accident. It describes the trip back through winter darkness and dangerous roads as an act of burial and care under conditions designed to deny both. The book’s story is not an independent archive record of every camp prisoner, but it shows how forced labor reached into Skala’s households.

Another order followed during Passover. On April 2, 1942, men were told to report in [Borshchiv](/communities/skala/records/mention_5651e24a0bb8d179eb2b32b2), and the book’s account says 84 were taken to a labor camp. The connected event record identifies the date as the first day of Passover. The wider record of Borshchiv adds that the town’s ghetto, formed in April 1942, later held Jews from several nearby communities, including Skala. This helps explain why Skala’s persecution cannot be told only within its municipal boundaries: displacement moved people into a regional system of confinement and mass murder. ([Borshchiv Ghetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borshchiv_Ghetto))

## The September 1942 Aktion

The memorial book marks September 26, 1942—the first day of Sukkot—as the start of a major action in Skala. Its account says the operation began at six in the morning, as families hid in cellars, attics and other improvised spaces. A connected record remembers [Michal Jagendorf](/communities/skala/records/mention_b961434c11d9953bbc2e7b18), a neighbor who warned people that something might happen. A child survivor’s later testimony also recalls warnings passed between streets and the community’s attempts to conceal hiding places. The testimony is another recollection, not an outside confirmation of every detail in the memorial book. ([Menachem Bartel’s testimony](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/SkalaPodol/Bartel.html))

The book names German personnel involved in searches and violence, including [Wilhelm Pfeiffer](/communities/skala/records/mention_0fea5e79d7b65c1e94aba410), and describes police forces surrounding the town. One record estimates about 150 gendarmes and police in the encirclement and search. The book also identifies the Gestapo and Kripo among the occupation forces. These details describe Skala’s operation locally; they should not be confused with the entire Nazi apparatus or treated as a complete roster of those involved.

The memorial book says women, older people and children were deported to Bełżec, the German killing center, while others were shot or taken away. It does not explicitly identify each person sent there, so the fate of particular individuals should not be inferred from the general account. The [Borshchiv Aktion](/communities/skala/records/event_candidate_082f70a7bc737b012ffc1c74) of June 5, 1943, is another episode in this regional sequence: the record says many Skala residents were killed in Borshchiv. The broader account of the Borshchiv ghetto describes additional deportations and shootings in 1943, including the liquidation of the ghetto. That context supports the memorial book’s picture of Skala residents being caught up in violence beyond their hometown, though it does not independently verify each Skala-specific detail. ([Borshchiv Ghetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borshchiv_Ghetto))

## What the wider record adds—and what it cannot settle

The town’s later record is not a full accounting of its victims. Yad Vashem’s published list of Pages of Testimony, for example, includes Rozia Stock, resident of Skala Podolska, recorded as having died in Skala in 1943. This is an individual name in a memorial record, not a complete census of the dead, and the surname alone does not establish her relationship to the Stock family described in the book. ([Yad Vashem list](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/pdf-drupal/en/download/remembrance/country/POLAND.pdf))

The town article on Wikipedia similarly notes that many Skala Jews perished in the Borshchiv ghetto and that the castle area was used as a forced-labor camp. These are useful regional pointers, but they do not replace the named testimony in the memorial book or archival research into individual lives. A further comparison with the nearby community of [Mielnica-Podilska](research:Jewish survivors from Skala displaced to the Borshchiv ghetto and their later fates) may clarify how the ghetto brought neighboring communities together—and how survivors’ routes diverged. ([Skala-Podilska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skala-Podilska))

The end of occupation did not restore the community. One record dates Soviet liberation to March 1944; another gives March 23, 1944, and says only a few Jews survived. The difference is one of precision, not necessarily contradiction: March is the month-level account, while March 23 is the specific date recorded elsewhere. The memorial book also says that Soviet forces later retreated and the town was overrun. Its concluding image is therefore not a return to the prewar world, but a devastated town in which only a small number of Jewish survivors remained.
